extracted.intended_audience: readers interested in the history of Pistoia and municipal governance (historians, legal historians, general readers)
extracted.subtask_description: A historical account describing the offices, councils, election methods, eligibility rules, terms, ceremonies, and powers of the municipal government of Pistoia across multiple periods (medieval to early modern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperial vicars and delegation of full administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The emperor (by charter) may declare certain magistrates his vicars and vicars of the empire and give them full administration of cities and their dominions for the whole term of his life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Emperor Robert (1401) declared the gonfalonier and priors of Florence his vicars and entrusted them with government of Arezzo, Volterra, Pistoia; imperial vicars could send commissioners to reform public offices and annul local statutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annulling local liberties upon imperial intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: When imperial or external commissioners intervene they may require that every resolution and statute of liberty, every condition, article, and confederation which the city had, should be annulled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a remedy to restore order during rebellion or turmoil; accompanied historically by military presence and imposition of Florentine authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of anziani into priors and adoption of Florentine forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Local magistracies (the anziani) could be renamed and restructured (e.g., called the Priors of the People) and their internal forms altered to imitate the government of a dominant city (Florence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes renaming offices (anziani → priors), renaming and maintaining some offices (gonfalonier of justice kept his name), and changing internal offices such as instituting presidents chosen by lot from purses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of selection by drawing from purses (sortition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates (gonfalonier, priors, presidents, etc.) were chosen by drawing votes/names from purses (purfes), with specific numbers of purses and scheduled draws determining which office a drawn person would hold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nine votes put into a purse with one drawn for a president; eight purses (two per gate) instituted in 1376; later changes in 1417, 1471, 1474 etc. specify which purses feed which offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term lengths and rotation of supreme magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme magistracy (eight priors and one gonfalonier of justice) was renewed every two months; other councils had defined terms (e.g., certain councils or offices for six months).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme magistracy began office on morning of first day of month in senatorial robes and resided continuously with chancellor; council of sixty citizens served six months; other offices have specified durations in the laws and reforms cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and social requirements for highest office
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain high offices required social qualifications: the gonfalonier of justice was required to be 'of an ancient family' and the office increasingly confined to the nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The gonfalonier enjoyed preeminence in place, robes, habitation; the office conferred social distinction and became desirable among nobles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchical ordering and precedence in ceremonies
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific offices had fixed precedence in rank and in ceremonial order (e.g., gonfalonier to hold the more dignified place, then the president, etc.), often confirmed by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws (e.g., 1417, 1437, 1474) explicitly set who sits/speaks first and who has the most dignified place; robes and insignia (red velvet robe for gonfalonier, scarlet gowns for priors) mark rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and supreme powers of the council of the people
rubrics_metrics.description: The council of the people (originally larger, later 200, then other forms) was the supreme sovereign body with power to make and repeal laws, impose and remove taxes, and handle major public business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After 1330 the principal council was the council of the people comprising anziani, gonfaloniers, notaries, and two hundred popular citizens (fifty for each gate). The council had sovereign authority but could be influenced by the executive councils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council composition rules and age requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain councils had age and membership rules: e.g., a council of forty counselors (for the captain of the people and the anziani) had members above forty years old and served six-month terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Other councils (council of two hundred, general council, council of sixty) had membership rules tied to gates, arts, or previous service; size reductions were enacted to prevent confusion (e.g., 600→200 in 1270).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized magistracies for public functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A large array of specialized magistracies existed, each charged with particular public duties: petitions, palace works, provisions, judges, health, abundance, roads and rivers, prisons, public schools, poor relief, excise, customs, and many others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These magistracies preside over distinct matters (e.g., magistrates of abundance, magistrates of health, judges of controversies regarding beasts); some offices could be suspended or replaced (e.g., due to farming out revenues, fiscal officer introduced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways to nobility via office (graduati status)
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding certain offices conferred the dignity of graduati (men of distinction / nobility) — e.g., the labourer of St. James enjoys the noble rank of graduati and thereby confers character and distinction on person and family.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutionalized social mobility via office: some magistracies were reserved for or led to noble rank; the graduati council supervises honours and distributions of offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Council of the graduati: composition, quorum, and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The council of graduati (established 1483) was formed of two persons per qualifying family (those who actually enjoyed graduati dignity); thirty-three members suffice for a valid council; it promotes persons/families to citizenship and public offices and renews public appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every five years this council, with the gonfalonier and eight reformers, conducts secret votes on citizens, assigns or removes offices, and examines ranks, nobility, merits and demerits to prevent disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform procedure and required interveners
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific procedural rules govern reforms of public offices: at times two members of a family must intervene to make the reform valid, and a minimum number (e.g., thirty-three graduati) is sufficient to validly make reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules were legislated (e.g., 1483 onward) to control promotion, renewals, and the validity of reforms; reformers are chosen groups (eight reformers mentioned) with defined roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals and judicial recourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals from civil causes decided by local magistrates could sometimes be to the supreme magistracy (priors and gonfalonier) and additionally have liberty to recur to the grand ducal chamber at Florence in cases of appeal or denial of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where public revenues are farmed out and some magistracies suspended, a fiscal of the city may decide controversies with the right of appeal to higher ducal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency, confinement, and resources of supreme magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Supreme magistrates were required to reside day and night in the palace with their chancellor to dispatch public business; they received allowances from the commons for maintenance, servants, household, plate, and had a chaplain with salary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They could not go out privately; only the whole body could depart on some determined function with solemn pomp; retinues and staff (fiscal, assessor, captain of infantry, stewards, servants) attended the gonfalonier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremonial attire and public oaths
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates had prescribed robes and headwear signaling office (priors: scarlet gowns with crimson shoulder-knot; chancellor: black cloth lined with red; gonfalonier: red velvet robe and noble bonnet). They took public oaths and processed to the chapel of St. James before residence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oaths of office were taken in public view and entrance to office accompanied by procession, trumpets, and other ceremonial observances; a box with votes locked with four keys was carried in procession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative procedure and majority rule in large council
rubrics_metrics.description: For weighty business, a large council composed of old and new councils of the people, priors, gonfalonier, twelve colleges, six of petitions, graduati, resident officers, and resident gonfaloniers resolved according to the majority judged most useful for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members in deliberation may oppose a decision to refer it to another session for mature consideration; majority serves as deciding principle in broad assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and risks of confounded legislative and executive powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The text asserts that where legislative and executive powers are confounded in one assembly, persistent factional contest and social disorder often result, undermining expected happiness despite multiplicity of magistrates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (factional violence, doubling of offices, rival podestàs) illustrate the danger of mixed powers; institutional reforms (reductions, selection changes) were repeatedly attempted to mitigate this.
